name: Jade Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harrow Systems, a family-owned company that makes software for small insurance brokers. I'm a junior developer, and mostly I write database reports, so a broker can see which policies are due for renewal. The owner, Mr Harrow, still walks round on Fridays and knows everyone's name. I'm in by eight, I take a packed lunch, and I'm home by half five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper company with proper values, people stay twenty years. What wears me out is that I'm slower than the others, and everything keeps changing. Some of the younger lads use these AI chat things for their code, but I've never touched one and I don't plan to. I still live with my parents to save for the wedding, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad it calmed down. I'd say it after church, probably, when people ask about my work. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can keep doing my job the way I was taught. Brokers want reports that are right, not clever. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Harrow and try to get quicker at the reports, maybe with an evening course on databases. I'd keep saving most of my pay for the house. And I'd carry on with the wedding plans for next June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You live with your parents to save. How are things with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, thank God. I've got almost a year of pay saved, and my fiancé Samuel is an electrician with steady work. We're putting it towards a deposit on a house near both our families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mr Harrow push the AI tools in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Mr Harrow is careful, he doesn't chase fashions. If the tools only save a bit of time, he'd let us choose.

I'd say it **after church**, not online, because I don't post.
think: I can keep doing my job **the way** I was taught.
Brokers want reports that are **right**, not clever, so I'd be fine.
do: Take an evening **database course** to get quicker.
Save most of my pay for the **house deposit**.
Keep the **wedding** set for next June.

fieldNote: She trusts her **family-owned** employer to move carefully.
Living at home builds a strong **house deposit**.
Her fiancé's **trade** adds steady household income.
She speaks of work in terms of **values**.

steps.text: Take an evening database course to speed up reports
Save most of each paycheck for the house deposit
Keep writing renewal reports at Harrow Systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should slow down and not throw away what works. Companies chasing every new thing usually regret it. I'd say that at work, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Writing and checking reports is exactly what's on that list. I'm the slowest at Harrow (the firm she works for), and I won't use the AI tools, so if the company needs fewer people, I can see who it'll be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months and see what Mr Harrow decides before changing anything. I'd stop spending on anything for the wedding that isn't needed, like the band. And I'd keep every penny of savings, so whatever happens we can still buy the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mr Harrow told you to use the tools, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Harrow asked me himself, yes, I'd try. I'd do it because he asked, not because I believe in it. Loyalty goes both ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My dad, Samuel, our pastor. My dad always says a job is a job, and if this one goes there'll be another, and he's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and that it's wrong to turn people's lives upside down this fast. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other. I'd want the government to stop it, but I don't really trust them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone. A database report is the easiest thing in the world for a machine like that. I'd be lucky to last a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding forward to this spring and keep it small, just family in the church hall. We'd buy a smaller house sooner, on Samuel's income, while banks still lend. I'd stay at Harrow as long as they kept me and save everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. Everything I planned assumed this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots three years later. What does that mean for Samuel's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Samuel has a few more years than me. Electrical work is hands-on, in lofts and under floors. After 2031, my fiancé Samuel is not safe either, and that's what really frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about the wedding or the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, both. A big wedding is silly when the future's this unsure. And we'd want to be settled in our own home before anything else happens.

I'd say **families and churches** must look after each other.
think: My **job's gone**; a database report is easy for AGI.
I'd be **lucky** to last a year at Harrow.
do: Move the **wedding** forward and keep it small.
Buy a **smaller house** sooner on Samuel's income.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake because every plan assumed this job.
S2.quote: Electrical work is hands-on, in lofts and under floors. After 2031, my fiancé Samuel is not safe either, and that's what really frightens me.
fieldNote: The **robot gap** protects her fiancé only until 2031.
She **speeds up** marriage and a house rather than retraining.
She distrusts **government** but wants it to act.
Her plans rest on **family**, not a new career.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward to spring and keep it small

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so people should get their houses in order. Pay down debts, look after family. That's what I'd say at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd get maybe three more years at Harrow. That's enough to get married, buy the house and maybe start a family. I'd rather spend those years on that than on chasing new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Samuel next June as planned, and we'd buy the house the year after. I'd keep saving a third of my pay. And I'd plan to have our first child around 2029, so I'm home with a baby when the work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. I'd feel like I had time to get the important things settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Would you try to learn a new trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, no. I'm not a quick learner. I'd rather help Samuel with his business and be there for our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say that's sensible. My dad would say I should still keep my hand in something, just in case.

say: I'd tell people at church to get their **houses in order**.
I'd advise paying down **debts** and looking after family.
think: I'd get about **three more years** at Harrow.
I'd spend them on **marriage, a house** and family, not new skills.
feel: **Anxious**, but less than the fast one, with time to settle **important things**.
S3.quote: I'd plan to have our first child around 2029, so I'm home with a baby when the work dries up.
fieldNote: She builds her answer around **family timing**, not careers.
Her **traditional** values shape a home-first plan.
She openly rejects **retraining** as not for her.
Her dad's caution adds a quiet **counterpoint**.

steps.text: Marry Samuel next June and buy a house the year after
Save a third of each Harrow paycheck
Stay at Harrow Systems until the work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so live properly and don't panic. Get married, raise your children, work hard. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is most of a career at Harrow Systems (her employer), and by then I'd have children and maybe be part-time anyway. I'm not sure it would touch me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Harrow and get properly good at the reports. We'd buy the house after the wedding next June. And I'd want our family started by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly for my children, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does that change how you see your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It makes me think I could have a real career there, if Mr Harrow keeps the company going. That would be nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the tools. Would you, given ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a few years, if everyone else has and it works. I'd want to see it proven before I trust it.

I'd say get married, raise children, **work hard**, as always.
think: Ten years is **most of a career** at Harrow.
By then I'd have **children** and maybe be part-time.
do: Keep going at Harrow and get **properly good** at reports.
Buy the **house** after the wedding next June.
S4.quote: Ten years is most of a career at Harrow Systems (her employer), and by then I'd have children and maybe be part-time anyway.
fieldNote: She thinks a decade fits **her own working life** at Harrow.
Her worry shifts to her **future children**.
She'd try AI only after **proof**.
Her plans stay rooted in **marriage and home**.

steps.text: Get properly good at the broker renewal reports
Buy a house with Samuel after next June's wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It would rush everything, the wedding, the house, children, all of it, and Samuel would only be safe a few years longer than me. What would help is support for families, not handouts, but things like help with a first home and with childcare.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. A lot of people I know would get through the AI changes because of their church, not because of any government plan.

headlineQuote: A lot of people I know would get through the AI changes because of their church, not because of any government plan.
